title: A Postcards for the Aftermath
premise: Oscar Nystrom, a night librarian drifting through an insomniac city, is summoned by Ilse Varga, the last fluent speaker of Kessari, who wants one final student before she dies. As he learns the language, he discovers it holds no word for 'duty' but fourteen words for kinds of love — and that Ilse spent decades translating testimony from a massacre her own family helped commit. The untranslatable sentence she asks him to render is her confession, and publishing it means betraying the descendants who paid him to keep it silent. In the end Oscar chooses memory over protection: he translates the sentence into Kessari itself, speaks it aloud at her funeral where no one else can understand it, and keeps the truth alive in the only tongue that can hold it.
about_author: A. M. Underhill is the pen name of a former archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing endangered-language recordings in northern Europe. They now write fiction about the people history leaves holding its paperwork.

chapters.title: The Night Shift of Languages
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Working nights in a library that never fully closes, Oscar receives a letter requesting access to the restricted Kessari archive — signed by a woman presumed dead for thirty years. He finds Ilse Varga waiting among the stacks at 3 a.m., sharp and dying. She offers to teach him the language if he'll take dictation. Beat: reluctant curiosity displacing his numbness.

chapters.title: Fourteen Words for Love
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Oscar's lessons and Ilse's dictation sessions. He learns Kessari has no word for duty, and she begins dictating fragments of testimony from the Vellmark massacre — including names of perpetrators, her family among them. A lawyer representing the victims' descendants contacts Oscar, warning him off. Beat: wonder curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: The Sentence That Won't Cross Over
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV, weakening in voice as the chapters progress. She dictates the final sentence — her full confession — and demands Oscar translate it into English for publication. The descendants offer him money to destroy the recording; Ilse's grandson begs him to honor her 'real' legacy instead. Torn between duty and love, Oscar stalls until Ilse collapses. Beat: the weight of being made executor of someone's guilt.

chapters.title: What Only the Dead Can Hear
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Ilse dies before he can promise anything. At her funeral, facing both the descendants and the lawyer, Oscar rises and delivers the confession aloud — in Kessari, untranslated, with Ilse's recordings playing beneath. The guilty are named in a language almost no one living can hear, yet the archive is public forever. He returns to the night shift changed: a tenant no longer. Beat: grief transmuted into witness.
